claims: Price elasticity measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded or supplied to the product’s own price change using a ratio of percentage changes.
Elastic means a responsiveness magnitude above one; inelastic below one; unit elastic equals one; perfectly inelastic equals zero.
Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold; it differs from profit because costs are not subtracted.
For price inelastic demand over the relevant change, a price rise increases total revenue because the proportionate quantity fall is smaller than the price increase.
Close substitutes, necessity, budget share and adjustment time can affect demand responsiveness, while spare capacity, stocks and production time can affect supply responsiveness.
Elasticity coefficients are ratios rather than percentages, money amounts or counts of units.
Percentage changes must use the stated reference values consistently before quantity change is divided by price change.
Price elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
The usual negative demand relationship can give a negative signed coefficient; demand responsiveness is commonly classified by its magnitude.
Price elasticity of supply is the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
Supply responsiveness depends on the period available and ability to adjust offered output rather than the absolute size of the price change alone.
Using initial values, demand elasticity magnitude equals the absolute value of ((new quantity minus initial quantity)/initial quantity) divided by ((new price minus initial price)/initial price).
A 12 percent fall in quantity demanded following an 8 percent price rise gives demand elasticity magnitude 1.5, classified elastic.
Using initial values, supply elasticity equals ((new quantity minus initial quantity)/initial quantity) divided by ((new price minus initial price)/initial price).
A 5 percent increase in quantity supplied following a 10 percent price rise gives supply elasticity 0.5, classified inelastic.

CU-6145-3.3:
Price elasticity measures how strongly quantity demanded or supplied responds to a change in the product’s own price. Comparing percentage changes makes the measure independent of whether quantities are counted in individual items or hundreds. A fall of ten units could be large for a seller initially selling twenty but small for one initially selling a thousand. The percentage change supplies the needed reference. Divide the percentage quantity change by the percentage price change; do not reverse the ratio.

Classify responsiveness by the coefficient’s magnitude. Elastic means above one: the percentage quantity response is larger than the percentage price change. Inelastic means below one: it is smaller. Unit elastic means equal percentage changes, giving one. Perfectly inelastic means zero quantity response, giving zero. Merely inelastic demand can still change quantity; it is not necessarily perfectly inelastic. These categories describe responsiveness over the relevant change and under the stated conditions. They do not mean that a whole product category has one unchanging coefficient in every market and time period. Use evidence about price and quantity rather than guessing the classification from whether the price looks expensive.

Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. It is the money received from sales before costs are subtracted, so it is not profit. When demand is price inelastic for the relevant change, raising price increases total revenue because the quantity sold falls proportionately less than price rises. For price elastic demand the loss of quantity can instead outweigh the higher price, reducing revenue. Unit elasticity means equal proportional responsiveness. For finite initial-value examples, calculate the actual revenue from both price-quantity pairs rather than assuming an exact offset. Perfectly inelastic demand has no quantity response over the assumed change, but that is a special case rather than a description of most ordinary products.

Consider an invented stall increasing price from N$20 to N$22 while weekly sales fall from 100 to 95. Revenue moves from N$2,000 to N$2,090. Using initial values, price rises 10 percent and quantity falls 5 percent, giving demand elasticity magnitude 0.5, inelastic. The revenue increase is N$90; costs have not been supplied, so a profit conclusion would be unsupported. A different sales response could reverse the conclusion. The example demonstrates why a price rise alone is not a complete pricing argument. A firm needs evidence about the relevant buyers and should consider whether their response changes as they find alternatives over time.

Close alternatives can make demand more price responsive because buyers can switch when one product becomes dearer. A necessity with few substitutes may have less responsive demand. Budget share can matter: a large expense creates more incentive to search for alternatives than a very small one. Adjustment takes time, so people may have greater ability to change habits or equipment in the longer term. These factors support a reasoned tendency rather than a guaranteed coefficient. A named product without case evidence is insufficient to establish a precise elasticity value.

Supply responsiveness depends on how easily producers can alter the amount offered. Spare capacity, available inputs and inventories can support a faster response. Production requiring long growing or construction periods may be difficult to expand immediately. A workshop with unused machines may offer substantially more after a price rise; a harvest already determined by the season may change little in the immediate period. The distinction is quantity response to own price, not a supply shift caused by new technology. Price changes move along the relevant relationship; changes in production conditions can alter that relationship. Keep the comparison period clear when applying either concept.

An elasticity coefficient is a ratio, not a percentage. If quantity changes by 12 percent and price by 8 percent, dividing gives a magnitude of 1.5. The percentage signs belong to the changes being compared, not to the final coefficient. Saying elasticity is 1.5 percent would mislabel it. A coefficient of 0.5 means the proportionate quantity response is half the proportionate price change, not that quantity is half a unit or price is fifty cents.

Use a consistent reference basis. These worked examples use initial price and quantity as their bases, and prompts state that convention. If a question gives percentage changes directly, divide those percentages rather than calculating another percentage from the coefficient. If the price change is zero, the simple ratio has a zero denominator and cannot provide an ordinary numerical coefficient. Explain the missing information rather than invent a result. This topic links to market forces in 3.2 and pricing policies in 3.5: responsiveness helps explain the effect of a price decision, while demand and supply shifts explain changes in the underlying market conditions. A comparison should name both the percentage response and the underlying side of the market. Two coefficients may have the same numerical value while describing different economic agents. Evidence about buyers cannot be silently substituted for evidence about producers.
CU-6145-3.3.1:
Price elasticity of demand is the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. The quantity refers to buyers’ plans. The measure asks how strongly those plans respond to the product’s own price, with other relevant conditions unchanged. If price rises and quantity demanded falls, the signed ratio is negative. For classification, these examples report the absolute magnitude and explain the direction separately. State this convention so a negative sign is not confused with an inelastic classification.

A demand coefficient with magnitude two is elastic, while one with magnitude one half is inelastic. It is the distance from zero relative to one that matters, not whether a negative signed number is numerically less than one. For example, a signed coefficient of minus two has magnitude two and is elastic. Perfectly inelastic demand instead has a zero quantity response over the assumed change. Unit elastic demand has equal proportionate changes. All four distinctions concern responsiveness, rather than how much a household likes the product. Strong desire does not establish ability to pay or a zero response to price. A full application uses the available alternatives, budget circumstances and time period in the case to support the likely responsiveness. A useful test is to compare two equal percentage price changes. If one group reduces quantity by 15 percent after a 5 percent price rise and another by 2 percent, their magnitudes are three and 0.4. The first response is elastic and the second inelastic. The number of physical units initially purchased is not enough to classify either response.

Price elasticity of supply is the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price. Here the quantity belongs to producers’ planned offers, not buyers’ purchases. In the usual positive supply relationship, higher price encourages greater quantity supplied, giving a positive ratio. Elastic supply responds more than proportionately, inelastic less than proportionately, and unit elastic in equal proportions. A perfectly inelastic supply case has no quantity response in the stated period.

Time and capacity are central to application. An invented sandwich producer with ingredients and unused equipment may expand the amount offered relatively quickly. A grower cannot instantly produce a new season’s crop merely because today’s price rises. Existing stocks might allow more immediate sales, but future production still takes time. These are reasons for differences in responsiveness, not proof of exact coefficients. Demand and supply elasticities must also stay separate: buyers having many alternatives does not directly measure the producer’s capacity to expand. Conversely, spare factory capacity does not tell us how buyers react to a price rise. Link each explanation to the side of the market whose quantity is changing. This connects to the main unit’s calculation: choose the correct quantity before dividing by the price change, then interpret the coefficient for that side and period. The period is part of the comparison rather than a decorative detail. A producer may initially use stock, later arrange overtime and eventually expand capacity. Each step changes what adjustments are feasible. The statement that supply is inelastic today does not mean that producers never respond or that the future coefficient must remain identical.
CU-6145-3.3.3:
For an initial-value calculation, find the percentage quantity change as the quantity difference divided by initial quantity, multiplied by 100. Do the same for price. Then divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change. To classify demand responsiveness, use the magnitude of that ratio. Keeping the percentage calculations visible helps identify an incorrect starting value or a reversed division. The final coefficient has no currency or physical unit.

At an invented bag seller, price rises from N$50 to N$54 while weekly quantity demanded falls from 250 to 220. Quantity change is minus 30; minus 30 divided by 250 times 100 gives minus 12 percent. Price change is N$4; 4 divided by 50 times 100 gives 8 percent. The signed ratio is minus 12 divided by 8, or minus 1.5; magnitude is 1.5, elastic. Revenue changes from N$12,500 to N$11,880, a fall of N$620. This supports the interpretation that the quantity loss outweighed the higher price in this example. Do not label the coefficient 1.5 percent. A result mark can be awarded for the requested coefficient even though the teaching explanation shows several steps. The steps are learning support, not extra marks added to the stated tariff. Before calculating, write the initial and new values in pairs so price is not divided by quantity accidentally. After calculating, check whether the magnitude agrees with the percentage comparison: a 12 percent quantity response is larger than an 8 percent price response, so a result below one would signal an error. This independent sense check supports the arithmetic without replacing interpretation of the economic result.

Use quantity supplied, rather than demanded, in a supply calculation. Suppose an invented basket producer increases weekly offers from 400 to 420 when price rises from N$30 to N$33. Quantity rises by 20, which is 20 divided by 400 times 100, or 5 percent. Price rises by N$3, which is 3 divided by 30 times 100, or 10 percent. Supply elasticity is 5 divided by 10, or 0.5. Supply is inelastic for this change: the quantity response is proportionately smaller than the price increase. The coefficient is neither N$0.50 nor 0.5 baskets.

The calculation describes the stated observations under the assumed unchanged conditions. It does not prove the producer is incapable of a larger response next year, or establish why this response occurred without additional evidence. Limited spare capacity could be a possible explanation if the case states it. A different calculation with a 30 percent quantity response to a 10 percent price change gives three, elastic; a 10 percent quantity response gives one, unit elastic. Compare the ratios rather than absolute unit changes. This links the worked supply calculation to the demand example: both divide percentage quantity change by percentage price change, but the quantity and economic interpretation belong to different sides of the market. Use consistent initial values and state the time period in the original data. If percentages are already provided, no initial-value reconstruction is needed. For example, a supplied 6 percent quantity increase and 12 percent price increase give 0.5 directly. Retain enough figures during intermediate calculations to avoid changing a boundary classification through rounding. State the requested coefficient clearly, then use words to distinguish a smaller positive response from a zero response.

cards: Define price elasticity as a general measure for demand or supply.
Responsiveness of quantity demanded or supplied to own price, measured as a ratio of percentage quantity change to percentage price change.
Definition: quantity responsiveness 1; qualifier: ratio to own-price percentage change 1.
Identify the elasticity category with a coefficient magnitude of one.
Unit elastic (1).
Characteristic: unit elastic, 1.
Explain why a demand coefficient magnitude of 0.4 is not perfectly inelastic.
It shows a non-zero quantity response (1), so it is inelastic but not perfectly inelastic, which requires zero (1).
Context: 0.4; reasoning: non-zero response 1; result: ordinary inelastic classification 1.
Define total revenue.
Money received from sales, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold before costs are subtracted.
Meaning: sales receipts 1; distinguishing feature: price times quantity, not profit 1.
Explain how a price rise affects total revenue when demand is price inelastic over the relevant change.
Initial change: price rises (1); with inelastic demand the quantity fall is proportionately smaller, so total revenue increases (1).
Initial change: price rise 1; mechanism/effect: smaller proportionate quantity loss under inelastic demand raises revenue 1.
Explain why a producer with spare equipment and available inputs may have more price-responsive supply than one already at full capacity in the same short period.
The first producer can expand offered output using unused resources (1), so its quantity can respond more strongly to a price incentive than the capacity-constrained producer’s (1).
Context: different spare capacity; reasoning: adjustment feasible 1; result: stronger potential response 1.
Explain what demand elasticity magnitude 2 means when based on a 20 percent quantity fall following a 10 percent price rise.

Quantity responds twice as strongly in percentage terms as price. The evidence is 20 divided by 10 equals 2. Demand is elastic, so the proportionate quantity loss is larger than the price increase; the coefficient is a ratio, not 2 percent.
Relationship: twice proportionate response 1; evidence: 20/10 1; explanation: elastic and ratio rather than percentage 2.
Explain why a demand coefficient of 1.2 should not be written as 1.2 percent.
It divides a percentage quantity change by a percentage price change (1), producing a ratio with no percent unit (1).
Context: 1.2 result; reasoning: percentage ratio 1; result: dimensionless coefficient 1.
Define price elasticity of demand.
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
Definition: buyer quantity response 1; qualifier: divided by percentage price change 1.
Define price elasticity of supply.
The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a price change, measured by percentage change in quantity supplied divided by percentage change in price.
Meaning: producer quantity response 1; qualifier: percentage-change ratio 1.
Calculate demand elasticity magnitude using initial values when price rises from N$50 to N$54 and weekly demand falls from 250 to 220 units.
Formula: magnitude of percentage quantity change divided by percentage price change. Working: quantity falls 12 percent; price rises 8 percent; magnitude = 12/8 = 1.5. Answer: coefficient 1.5.
Formula/working shown for learning; award the single result mark for answer coefficient 1.5.
Explain the interpretation of demand elasticity magnitude 1.5 calculated from a 12 percent quantity fall and an 8 percent price rise.

Demand is elastic because 1.5 exceeds one. The quantity fall is proportionately 1.5 times the price rise, as 12 divided by 8 shows. Buyers respond more than proportionately over this change, not by a fixed number of units per dollar.
Relationship: more than proportionate 1; evidence: 12/8 and above-one coefficient 1; explanation: elastic, relative not absolute measure 2.
Explain why an initial-value demand calculation must divide the change in weekly sales by the original sales quantity rather than the new quantity.
The initial-value convention measures the change relative to the starting amount (1), so using the new amount would use a different reference and alter the percentage (1).
Context: initial-value convention; reasoning: starting base 1; result: new base changes measure 1.
Calculate supply elasticity using initial values when weekly quantity supplied rises from 400 to 420 and price rises from N$30 to N$33.
Formula: percentage quantity supplied change divided by percentage price change. Working: 20/400 × 100 = 5 percent; 3/30 × 100 = 10 percent; 5/10 = 0.5. Answer: coefficient 0.5.
Formula and working for teaching; answer coefficient 0.5 earns the single result mark.
Explain what supply elasticity 0.5 means when quantity supplied rises 5 percent after price rises 10 percent.

Supply is inelastic because the coefficient is below one. The quantity response is half the proportionate price change, shown by 5 divided by 10. Output offered still rises, but less than proportionately; it is not perfectly inelastic or a decrease in supply.
Relationship: half the proportionate response 1; evidence: 5/10=0.5 1; explanation: inelastic positive response, not zero or shift 2.
Explain why using customer purchases instead of producers’ offered quantity would not calculate the stated supply elasticity.
Supply elasticity concerns the change in quantity producers offer (1), so substituting buyer quantity measures a different side of the market (1).
Context: supply calculation; reasoning: correct producer quantity 1; result: buyer quantity changes the measure 1.
Explain the error in calling demand inelastic when quantity falls 18 percent after price rises 6 percent.
The magnitude is 18/6=3, above one (1), so demand is elastic rather than inelastic because quantity responds more than proportionately (1).
Confusion: classification reversed; boundary/test: coefficient above one, 1 each for evidence and correct classification.
Explain the difference between a 3 percent quantity fall after a 10 percent price rise and no quantity change after that rise.
The first has magnitude 0.3 and is inelastic (1); the second has zero responsiveness and is perfectly inelastic (1).
Confusion: small response versus none; boundary/test: coefficient 0.3 versus zero, 1 each.
performance: data_response

The invented Reed Baskets stall raises price from N$40 to N$44. Weekly quantity demanded falls from 150 to 144. Other demand conditions are unchanged; use initial values. Costs are not supplied. Nearby sellers offer similar baskets. (a) Describe three features of the price and quantity data (6). (b) Examine the implications for responsiveness and revenue (7). (c) Suggest how the owner should use the result in deciding future prices (7).

(a) Price rises N$4, which is 10 percent. Quantity falls six baskets, which is 4 percent. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, with a proportionately smaller quantity response. (b) Demand elasticity magnitude is 4/10=0.4, inelastic for this change. Revenue rises from N$6,000 to N$6,336, an increase of N$336. The quantity loss is proportionately smaller than the price gain. This is revenue, not profit, because costs are absent. (c) Use the observed inelastic response as evidence for this particular change, but do not assume further rises behave identically. Similar sellers offer alternatives and buyers may switch after more time. Compare costs and longer-term quantity response before judging profitability. A cautious pricing review is defensible if it checks whether the observed response persists and whether the additional receipts exceed any relevant cost changes.

Context: Reed Baskets. Parts/allocation: (a) price pattern 2, quantity pattern 2, proportionate comparison 2 = 6. (b) coefficient/classification 2, revenue evidence 2, inelastic mechanism 2, profit boundary 1 = 7. (c) relevant evidence 2, substitutes/time 2, conditional judgement including costs 3 = 7.
short_answer

(a) Define price elasticity of demand (2). (b) Define price elasticity of supply (2). (c) Explain why a coefficient is not a percentage (2). (d) Explain the difference between inelastic and perfectly inelastic demand (2). (e) Explain one reason close substitutes can affect demand responsiveness (2). (f) Explain why available adjustment time can affect supply responsiveness (2). (g) Explain why total revenue is not profit (2). (h) Explain why a signed demand coefficient of minus two can be classified elastic (2).

(a) Percentage demand-quantity response divided by percentage price change. (b) Percentage supply-quantity response divided by percentage price change. (c) It is a ratio of two percentage changes, leaving no percentage unit. (d) Inelastic can have a small non-zero response; perfectly inelastic has none. (e) Alternatives let buyers switch when price rises, increasing potential response. (f) More time may allow producers to adjust capacity or output. (g) Revenue is sales receipts, while profit requires costs to be deducted. (h) Classification uses magnitude two, which exceeds one, rather than treating the negative sign as low responsiveness.

Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a/b) correct quantity side + price ratio; (c) ratio + no percent unit; (d) small response + zero boundary; (e) substitutes + switching mechanism; (f) time + capacity adjustment; (g) receipts + cost deduction; (h) magnitude + above-one classification.
case_analysis

The invented Frame Craft workshop raises price from N$80 to N$88. Weekly quantity demanded falls from 200 to 160 with other demand conditions unchanged. The workshop could offer more output because it has spare capacity, but buyers have several alternative suppliers. Use initial values and ignore charges. (a) Define total revenue (2). (b) Explain two reasons why demand and supply responsiveness could differ here (4). (c) Explain the price change’s effect on demand responsiveness and revenue using the data (7). (d) Discuss whether spare capacity alone justifies a further price rise (7).

(a) Sales receipts, price multiplied by quantity sold before cost deduction. (b) Buyer alternatives support switching and greater demand responsiveness. Spare workshop capacity supports the producer’s ability to alter output, a supply-side response. (c) Price rises 10 percent; quantity falls 20 percent. Demand elasticity magnitude is two, elastic. Revenue falls from N$16,000 to N$14,080, a reduction of N$1,920. The proportionately larger quantity loss outweighs the price increase. Spare capacity does not change that observed buyer response. (d) Capacity can help meet additional orders, but does not establish that buyers will place them at a higher price. The observed elastic response and alternatives caution against assuming extra revenue. Another price rise needs evidence about the relevant demand response and costs; unused equipment alone is insufficient. The decision should prioritise buyer response and the objective sought, without claiming revenue equals profit. Inelastic demand for a proposed change could support a higher-revenue argument, but the observed response here is elastic and supports the opposite warning.

Context: Frame Craft. Parts/allocation: (a) sales receipts 1, price-times-quantity before costs 1. (b) demand substitute mechanism 2, supply capacity mechanism 2 = 4. (c) percentage evidence 2, coefficient/classification 2, revenue amounts and causal interpretation 3 = 7. (d) capacity benefit 2, demand-side limitation 2, supported judgement distinguishing revenue/profit and sides 3 = 7.
essay_plan

Evaluate whether an invented refill station should infer that a price rise will improve its financial performance solely because demand was inelastic in one short trial; costs and longer-term responses are unknown (9).

For: inelastic demand in the relevant trial means the quantity loss was proportionately smaller than the price rise, increasing total revenue for that change. This provides useful evidence about short-run buyer behaviour. Against: buyers may find substitutes over time, and a larger price change may have a different response. Revenue does not measure profit without costs. A one-period result also does not establish the effect on all customers or future sales. Judgement: use the trial as limited evidence and compare repeat demand responses and costs before inferring improved financial performance. The condition is that relevant demand remains inelastic for the proposed change and the resulting receipts relative to costs support the objective. A coefficient alone is insufficient.

Argument for: inelastic condition and revenue mechanism, up to 4. Argument against: time/size limitations and profit distinction, up to 4. Judgement: distinct condition on relevant response and costs, 1. Total 9.
judgements: Initial-value convention and demand magnitude are explicit. No midpoint method is implied.
Parent DEF on applied objective uses total revenue, supporting application without duplicating PED/PES definitions.
Price-revenue mechanisms carry inelastic conditions; receipts are not assumed profit.

The broad conditioned-mechanism detector also matched the elastic-demand case. Its answer includes a substantive contrasting inelastic case while retaining the actual elastic conclusion; no condition was falsely applied to the data.
Finite initial-value calculations use actual revenue products; unit-elastic classification is not used to assert an exact finite revenue offset.
